Moving to Green Bay, you'll find that the Packers connection is less a marketing gimmick than a genuinely unusual civic structure, though the intensity of the football culture is also very real day to day.

The team is the only non-profit, community-owned franchise in major American professional sports, run by an elected board of directors rather than a single wealthy owner. [shard_03173_47283]
No shareholder may hold more than 200,000 shares, a rule designed specifically to prevent any one person from taking control of the club, and the stock pays no dividends, cannot appreciate, and confers no season-ticket privileges. [shard_03173_47283]
This structure violates current NFL ownership rules, but Green Bay was grandfathered in when the league's modern ownership policy was adopted in the 1980s, making the Packers a permanent exception. [shard_03173_47283]
That ownership model is one reason often cited for why the team has never relocated despite Green Bay being by far the smallest market in the league. [shard_03173_47283]
On the economic side, estimates vary but consistently show the team as a meaningful, though not all-encompassing, driver of local activity: one study put the Packers' annual economic contribution around $160 million and roughly 2,500 supported jobs, while another analysis focused specifically on Lambeau Field found it adds about $282 million to the local economy, supports 2,560 jobs, and generates $15.2 million in local tax revenue. [shard_04075_34770] [shard_01626_69050]
The team's charitable arm, the Green Bay Packers Foundation, has donated more than $37 million to regional organizations since 1986, so the team's presence shows up in local nonprofit and community funding as well as game-day spending. [shard_04075_34770]
Importantly, Green Bay's broader economy is not solely football-dependent: paper manufacturing has long earned the region the nickname "Paper Valley," with major employers like Georgia-Pacific and Kimberly-Clark, alongside a diversified manufacturing base, a significant healthcare sector anchored by systems like Bellin Health and Aurora, retail employers, and higher education institutions such as UW-Green Bay. [shard_00581_50412]
So while the Packers are a visible and financially significant presence, most residents' paychecks and daily errands are not directly tied to the team. [shard_00581_50412]
Where the Packers really do saturate daily life is in local media and conversation: a longtime Green Bay sports radio host described his job as needing to find a Packers angle for every single show, 365 days a year, even in the dead of the NFL offseason, because "nothing in Green Bay plays like the Packers." [shard_03318_83975]
He also noted that statewide college football loyalty to the Wisconsin Badgers is much stronger in Madison or Milwaukee than in Green Bay, where the Packers dominate attention regardless of what part of the state a caller is from, and that a large share of listener calls actually come from out-of-state diehards rather than only locals. [shard_03318_83975]
That said, a Green Bay native writing about national media coverage pushed back hard on the "whole town shuts down for the game" narrative, pointing out that not everyone in Green Bay is a Packers fan, probably not even half, and that many residents move there for work rather than football, with televised images of "empty streets" often just showing the non-residential downtown banking district rather than evidence of citywide devotion. [shard_02148_27189]
This is a useful corrective for newcomers who aren't big NFL fans: the "you can't understand Green Bay without the Packers" framing is partly accurate civic history and partly amplified, simplified tourist and media shorthand.
The traditions around Lambeau Field are nonetheless deeply embedded and worth knowing, starting with the sellout streak, which has held since 1960, and the season-ticket waiting list, which is so long that a fan joining today could expect roughly a 40-year wait based on historical turnover rates, since about 99 percent of ticket holders renew each year. [shard_00414_75955] [shard_01446_79000]
Lambeau Field's capacity of 73,128 amounts to about 72 percent of Green Bay's own city population of roughly 101,000, and the team's 112,000-plus shareholders actually outnumber the city's residents, which helps explain why the market functions so differently from typical NFL economics. [shard_01446_79000]
The stadium's "Frozen Tundra" nickname comes with real lore, including a persistent belief that the field's underground heating system was deliberately shut off during the 1967 "Ice Bowl" against Dallas at minus-15 degrees to give Green Bay a cold-weather advantage, though the team maintains it was simple malfunction. [shard_00414_75955]
The "Lambeau Leap," in which players jump into the stands after touchdowns, began as an improvised celebration and was later formally grandfathered in as an exception to NFL taunting rules. [shard_00414_75955]
Even presidential politics has touched Lambeau history: in 1961, Vince Lombardi asked President John F. Kennedy to grant a military leave so star player Paul Hornung could play in the NFL Championship Game, which Kennedy approved. [shard_00414_75955]
On rivalries, expect Chicago and Minnesota to come up constantly: the Packers-Bears matchup, dating to 1921, is the oldest rivalry in NFL history, with Green Bay holding a series edge of roughly 100 wins to 95 losses and six ties, while the Packers-Vikings rivalry, running since 1961, sits at about 62-54-3 in Green Bay's favor. [shard_00642_29374]
Both rivalries carry real fan animosity beyond the field, so casual conversation about either team should be approached carefully in mixed company. [shard_00642_29374]
As for downsides of a one-team-dominant town, history offers a candid example: before defensive star Reggie White chose to sign there in 1993, many NFL free agents actively avoided Green Bay, with one former player calling it "Siberia" because of its small size, lack of diversity, and harsh winters, a reputation that made it hard for the franchise to attract talent for years. [shard_03094_54344]
That same combination of small-town scale, cold climate, and limited diversity that once deterred players is a realistic thing for any non-fan newcomer to weigh, independent of football, when thinking about long-term fit. [shard_03094_54344]
